question.worked_solution:
Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope ${m}_{1}$ of the line passing through the points $(2,3)$ and $(-4,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{2-3}{-4-2} \\  & =\frac{(-1)}{(-6)} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy

$$
m\cdot (\frac{1}{6})=-1\,⇒\,m=-6.
$$

We know that the line passes through the point $(4,-1).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-1) & =-6(x-4) \\ y+1 & =-6x+24 \\ y & =-6x+23\end{aligned}
$$
